Use a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with x along the beam axis, y across the beam depth, and z across the beam width.
Assume the beam is straight, prismatic, homogeneous, isotropic, and linearly elastic with Young's modulus E.
Assume small deformation and Euler-Bernoulli kinematics, so plane sections initially perpendicular to the beam axis remain plane and perpendicular to the axis after bending.
Assume the beam is subjected to bending about the z-axis by an internal bending moment M(x), with no axial force, no torsion, and negligible transverse shear effect on the normal bending stress.
Let the rectangular cross-section have width b in the z direction and height h in the y direction.
Place the origin of y at the centroidal neutral axis, so the outer fibers are at y = h/2 and y = -h/2.
The relevant response quantities are the normal bending stress, the bending strain, the curvature, and the neutral axis location.
The bending stress at an arbitrary fiber located at y is sigma_x(y) = -M(x) y / I_z, where I_z = b h^3 / 12 is the second moment of area about the z-axis.
The maximum absolute bending stress occurs at the outer fibers y = h/2 or y = -h/2 and equals |sigma|_max = |M(x)| h / (2 I_z) = 6 |M(x)| / (b h^2).
The neutral axis is the line y = 0, where the bending stress is zero.
The bending strain at fiber y is epsilon_x(y) = -M(x) y / (E I_z).
The curvature of the beam is kappa(x) = M(x) / (E I_z).
If M varies along the beam due to transverse loading, use the local internal bending moment at the cross-section of interest in the expressions above.
